papers.title: Dynamical-Model-Informed Stochastic Flow Matching for Global Probabilistic Subseasonal Forecasting of Means and Extremes
papers.abstract_en: Physics-based models provide skillful subseasonal forecasts but suffer from systematic biases, weakened teleconnections, and parameterized physics, while very large ensembles remain computationally expensive. Purely data-driven models also see too few realizations of the low-frequency modes that provide subseasonal predictability. We introduce methodname, a hybrid framework that converts modelshort subseasonal ensemble guidance into 90-member stochastic forecasts of weekly precipitation and 2 m temperature on a global 1-degree grid using a lead-aware flow-matching U-Net. Its stochastic prior initializes members with EOF perturbations conditioned on the Madden-Julian Oscillation, North Atlantic Oscillation, El Nino-Southern Oscillation, and lead week, allowing the learned flow to refine large-scale covariance rather than create it from white noise. On held-out 2021-2025 forecasts, empirical CRPS improves by 22.0% for precipitation and 25.6% for temperature in a same-initialization four-versus-four comparison, and by 32.2% and 34.0% in the 90-versus-four production comparison. Ablations across five training seeds show distinct gains from the structured prior and a learned error-variance pathway, with the prior contributing more. Verification over 120 observed-extreme cases shows positive CRPS skill, but the ensemble remains underdispersive, four-member upper quantiles are poorly resolved, and precipitation exceedance BSS is near neutral after week 1. Results support improved probabilistic skill and tail representation, but not calibrated operational rare-event probabilities. Case studies of the 2022 UK heatwave, 2023 California atmospheric rivers, and 2022 Pakistan floods illustrate the reach and limits of dynamically informed refinement.

papers.title: Lighthouse: On Building a Trustworthy Digital Assistant for Exploring History with Civil Rights Archives
papers.abstract_en: Artificial intelligence (AI), as a decision-support aid, provides new tools for studying history effectively using multimodal data, including text, images, and audio. We present, to our knowledge, the first digital assistant named Lighthouse--commonly called a chatbot--for exploring the Civil Rights period of the United States using data from South Carolina. From an AI perspective, the system's novelty lies in its guiding design principles of (a) focusing on trustworthiness of content and (b) by modeling and reducing potential harm to users from generated answers. It implements these with a neuro-symbolic approach that combines neural learning through a large language model (LLM) with rule-based symbolic solving, balancing risk of answers with generality of coverage. We evaluate Lighthouse with both factual objective questions that admit a single acceptable answer as well as subjective questions. For the latter, a dataset of subjective question-answer pairs (QAs) is created by discovering a "gold standard" by aggregating answers from independent experts. Lighthouse has access to over 18k primary sources from a range of collections and can be easily extended.

papers.title: baseVultra: Compact Nonlinear Recurrence with Reallocated Capacity
papers.abstract_en: Nonlinear recurrent networks remain useful for streaming sequence modeling, yet gated cell design is still dominated by LSTM and GRU. We study whether recurrent computation can be reallocated away from gate transforms and toward candidate generation. We propose baseVultra, a compact recurrent cell that concentrates the dense recurrent budget on a single H x H candidate-generation matrix, while replacing recurrent gate matrices with O(H) diagonal interactions. The candidate update combines this dense branch with two low-rank auxiliary branches, an EMA cache, and learnable output blending; the gates additionally receive lightweight second-order access to h_{t-2} through diagonal terms. On TinyShakespeare character-level language modeling, baseVultra achieves a validation loss of 1.594 in the compact one-layer 200K setting, compared with 1.604 for a parameter-matched LSTM and 1.616 for a parameter-matched GRU, while its dense recurrent matrix-vector computation is about 54% of GRU under matched hidden size for this configuration. On text8, a roughly 45x larger benchmark, baseVultra is competitive with full-gate cells (1.854 bpc vs. 1.849 for GRU and 1.837 for LSTM). On formal-language probes, the largest gains appear under constrained hidden-state capacity (0.991 vs. 0.761 GRU and 0.691 LSTM OOD2 accuracy on Counter at H=16) and vanish as hidden size grows. These results characterize where and when candidate-focused recurrent capacity allocation helps: the benefit is concentrated in compact regimes, while full-gate cells remain competitive at scale.

papers.title: The Cost of Saying Hello: An Empirical Study of Handshake Overhead in AI Agent Communication Protocols
papers.abstract_en: Every interaction between AI agents begins with a handshake: the initiating agent must locate its counterpart, learn what it can do, and establish a session before the first useful message can be sent. Surveys of agent communication protocols name handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, yet none report measurements. This paper presents the first empirical, phase-decomposed benchmark of the handshake in three major agent protocols: MCP (in both its 2025 initialize and 2026 discover eras), A2A, and ACP. Using each protocol's official SDK, we instrument every request for round trips, per-phase latency, wire bytes, and token cost across cold-start, warm-repeat, capability-mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios (N=50 per cell, on loopback and under an emulated 50 ms RTT). Round-trip count dominates handshake cost. A legacy MCP handshake takes three round trips and 230 ms at 50 ms RTT; A2A needs one round trip and 61.0 ms. papers.title: Do Machine Learning-Guided Proactive Full Capacity Protocols Mitigate Emergency Department Overcrowding? A Simulation-Based Evaluation
papers.abstract_en: Objective: Emergency department (ED) overcrowding threatens care quality, yet Full Capacity Protocols (FCPs) are typically activated only after crowding thresholds have been exceeded. This study evaluated whether machine learning-guided proactive FCP activation improves ED crowding control compared with conventional reactive activation. Materials and Methods: We developed and validated an integrated machine learning and discrete-event simulation framework representing ED patient flow and capacity management. An embedded machine learning model predicted hourly waiting-room crowding six hours ahead and triggered proactive FCP activation. Using empirically calibrated operational parameters from a large US hospital, we compared proactive and reactive deployment strategies over a 365-day simulation horizon with 10 independent replications. Outcomes included ED length of stay, wait time, percentage of time above the crowding threshold, number of FCP activations, and protocol duration. Results: Proactive deployment produced statistically significant reductions in the percentage of time above the crowding threshold and average protocol duration across all threshold settings. It also reduced crowding variability and extreme congestion events, resulting in smoother ED operations. Although proactive deployment generally improved ED length of stay and wait time, these differences were not statistically significant. Conclusion: Embedding machine learning predictions within an operational simulation enables proactive, prediction-guided capacity management before severe congestion develops. These findings support the feasibility and potential value of proactive FCP deployment as a decision-support strategy for improving ED crowding control and provide evidence to support prospective implementation in clinical practice.

papers.title: MCP vs CLI for AI Agents: A Comparative Analysis of Tool Integration Strategies for Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract_en: AI agents require interfaces to interact with external systems such as files, APIs, databases, and cloud services. Two competing paradigms have emerged: CLI (Command Line Interface), where agents execute shell commands directly, and MCP (Model Context Protocol), a structured JSON-RPC protocol providing governed, typed tool access. This paper presents a comparative analysis across 14 evaluation dimensions, supported by worked examples, security assessment against established compliance frameworks, and economic modeling. Our analysis indicates that CLI provides superior efficiency for single-user, local-only workflows, while MCP addresses requirements that CLI fundamentally cannot satisfy, including fine-grained access control, credential isolation, structured audit, and multi-tenant governance. We further examine how progressive disclosure techniques eliminate MCP's historical weakness (context window overhead), yielding token efficiency comparable to CLI while preserving its architectural benefits. A hybrid architecture is recommended for production systems. This analysis draws upon academic, government, and industry sources including NSA formal guidance (CSI U/OO/6030316-26), OWASP security standards, and economic modeling from BCG and Gartner.
